<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">{tomer.gafni,asaf.karnieli,yair.hanani}@intel.com</span>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art results in a wide range of applications, from natural language processing and computer vision to speech recognition.
However, as tasks become increasingly complex, model sizes continue to grow, posing challenges in latency and memory efficiency. To meet these constraints, post-training quantization has emerged as a promising solution. In this paper, we propose a novel hardware-efficient quantization and inference scheme that exploits hardware advantages with minimal accuracy degradation. Specifically, we introduce a <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">W4A8</span> scheme, where weights are quantized and stored using 4-bit integer precision, and inference computations are performed using 8-bit floating-point arithmetic, demonstrating significant speedups and improved memory utilization compared to 16-bit operations, applicable on various modern accelerators. To mitigate accuracy loss, we develop a novel quantization algorithm, dubbed Dual Precision Quantization (DPQ), that leverages the unique structure of our scheme without introducing additional inference overhead. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance (i.e., increased throughput) while maintaining tolerable accuracy degradation relative to the full-precision model.
The source code is publicly available at the Intel Neural Compressor <a href="https://github.com/intel/neural-compressor" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">repository</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of tasks, having a significant impact in numerous fields. In recent years, model sizes have grown significantly to better capture complex data structures, accommodate longer context lengths, and enhance overall model strength. While these large-scale models exhibit outstanding functionality, their immense size poses significant challenges for deployment, including high computational costs and memory demands. To address these issues and enable efficient inference, quantization techniques are essential.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Quantization methods can be broadly categorized into two approaches: quantization-aware training (QAT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and post-training quantization (PTQ) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. The former integrates quantization into the training process, typically requiring extensive retraining and/or fine-tuning while employing approximate differentiation techniques for the rounding operation. In contrast, PTQ quantizes a pre-trained model with significantly fewer resources, such as compute and data, and over a much shorter process. PTQ is particularly appealing for large-scale models, where full retraining or even fine-tuning is prohibitively expensive. PTQ has been successfully implemented for both language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and vision models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.
In this paper, we focus on PTQ as a practical solution for efficient deployment of massive models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">PTQ produces a smaller and faster model. Reducing the size of the model allows us to use less memory on hardware accelerators such as Nvidia GPUs and Intel HPUs and/or increase the maximum batch size. A smaller model also reduces the bandwidth required to move weights from memory, which is particularly important at low batch sizes and in auto-regressive decoding scenarios. In addition, if we quantize the activations, we can take advantage of hardware support for fast low-precision operations, where the matrix-multiplication computation can be performed 2x faster than 16-bit floating point arithmetic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Therefore, when considering PTQ, it is crucial to understand the different regimes of inference performance, which broadly fall into two categories: compute-bound inference, where performance is limited by computational throughput, and memory-bound inference, where the bottleneck in performance is the rate at which data is transferred from memory to processing cores. Memory-bound scenarios are especially typical at low batch size, where there are a small number of operations per byte of the loaded model.
In memory-bound cases, performance gains are typically achieved by reducing memory traffic rather than increasing compute power, as hardware compute units are often underutilized while waiting for data to be fetched from memory.
Taking this into account, two primary approaches are commonly used to accelerate and optimize DNN inference, as detailed next.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">FP8 quantization</span>: Recent AI accelerators, including NVIDIA H100 &amp; H200, AMD MI300X, and Intel Gaudi 2 &amp; 3, supports the FP8 numerical format <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. FP8 offers two key advantages over 16-bit floating-point (FP) formats: (i) cutting memory requirements in half, leading to better memory utilization and improved bandwidth efficiency; and (ii) reducing computational complexity, often doubling throughput compared to 16-bit FP operations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">INT4 quantization</span>: For even greater compression, INT4 quantization is a leading approach that balances high compression with acceptable accuracy degradation. Storing weights in only 4 bits significantly reduces memory consumption, allowing larger models to fit on fewer machines and to increase the batch size, while improving inference speed. The low-precision representation reduces the latency associated with transferring weights from memory to processing cores, further accelerating model inference.
Various works considered effective algorithms, including AWQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, GPTQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, QuaRot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, SqueezeLLm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, AdaRound <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, APQ-Vit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, NoisyQuant <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> and more <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
Some algorithms related to this work uses information from second-order derivatives of the error function to perform network pruning and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose a hybrid W4A8 scheme, that both stores weights in 4-bit precision (W4) accounting for the memory-bound regime, and performs the arithmetic in FP8 (A8), accounting for the compute-bound regime.
Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> proposed a W4A8 quantization scheme similar to the one presented in this paper. However, their approach quantizes activations to 8-bit integers (INT8), whereas our method employs FP8 for both activations and computations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">FP8 can be advantageous over INT8 in terms of model accuracy, as INT8 represents a uniform distribution of values, making it most effective when model weights and activations also follow a uniform distribution. However, this is rarely the case, as empirical studies show that pretrained neural network weights typically exhibit a zero-centered, normal-like distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>. In contrast, FP8, with its non-uniform distribution and higher dynamic range, better accommodates such data distributions while also providing higher precision for small values, and better captures outliers.
This advantage becomes even more significant when quantizing activations as well, since their distributions tend to be less uniform and contain more outliers compared to weight distributions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are as follows. 
<br class="ltx_break">1) We propose a novel quantization and inference scheme that effectively accelerates inference in both the compute-bound and memory-bound regimes. Our proposed W4A8 scheme significantly reduces memory consumption, enabling larger batch sizes for faster evaluation and generation. Additionally, all matrix multiplications are performed in FP8, leveraging the capabilities of modern AI accelerators to enhance both speed and efficiency. 
<br class="ltx_break">2) To preserve accuracy, we introduce a dedicated quantization algorithm tailored for this scheme: the Dual Precision Quantization (DPQ). DPQ is designed to minimize quantization errors, allowing us to maintain most of the accuracy of the original model on various tasks, without introducing any inference overhead. 
<br class="ltx_break">3) Group-Aware Reordering (GAR): To further mitigate accuracy degradation, we introduce a weight quantization strategy that prioritizes important weights without inference overhead. Notably, GAR is not limited to our specific setting; it is applicable to other quantization schemes, making it a versatile technique for improving the accuracy of quantized models without introducing additional overhead. Ablation studies further confirm its effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we conduct experiments on both language-vision and large language models across a range of tasks and sizes. Specifically, we evaluate our scheme on Llama-2 and Llama-3 models (7B to 70B) as well as the Qwen2-VL family (2B to 72B), comparing it against existing algorithms and alternative precision strategies. The results demonstrate significant throughput gains with minimal accuracy degradation compared to higher-precision schemes, while also achieving better accuracy than existing W4A8 schemes, validating the effectiveness of our approach.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we introduce the fundamentals of DNN quantization, establish the relevant notation for our scheme, and discuss the key challenges in PTQ.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Integer Quantization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Integer quantization maps high-precision numbers to discrete levels. The process can be formulated as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

<tr id="S2.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lceil{\cdot}\rfloor" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lceil{\cdot}\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the rounding-to-nearest-integer operator, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑿</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the high-precision FP tensor, and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{INT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>q</mi><mtext>INT</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{INT}}</annotation></semantics></math> is its <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-bit quantized integer counterpart. The parameters <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{I}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{I}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the scaling factor and zero-point, respectively, where the subscript <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> indicates the integer format.
This is known as <span id="S2.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">asymmetric</span> quantization, where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{max}}=\max(\boldsymbol{X})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑿</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{max}}=\max(\boldsymbol{X})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{min}}=\min(\boldsymbol{X})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝑿</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{min}}=\min(\boldsymbol{X})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\text{max}}-q_{\text{min}}=2^{n}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\text{max}}-q_{\text{min}}=2^{n}-1</annotation></semantics></math>. <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.1 Integer Quantization ‣ 2 Background ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> can be further simplified to <span id="S2.SS1.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">symmetric</span> quantization, where <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{I}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{I}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{max}}=-\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{min}}=\max|\boldsymbol{X}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝑿</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{max}}=-\boldsymbol{X}_{\text{min}}=\max|\boldsymbol{X}|</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\text{max}}-q_{\text{min}}=2^{n}-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mtext>min</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\text{max}}-q_{\text{min}}=2^{n}-2</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The dequantized tensor is represented as:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}=(\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{INT}}-z_{I})\cdot s_{I}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>q</mi><mtext>INT</mtext></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>I</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>I</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}=(\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{INT}}-z_{I})\cdot s_{I}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, weights are stored in 4-bit precision using asymmetric integer quantization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>FP8 Quantization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we describe the FP8 quantization scheme used in this paper, focusing on the E4M3 data type (4-bit exponent and 3-bit mantissa). This format is widely adopted for inference, as higher precision is generally more important than a large dynamic range, which is more relevant during training (particularly in the backward pass) where the E5M2 format is commonly used.
Similarly to integer quantization, FP8 quantization applies a scaling factor to map a high-precision tensor into the FP8 dynamic range, followed by a rounding operation to the nearest representable value in the FP8 grid. We employ symmetric quantization. The process can be mathematically expressed as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{FP}}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{\boldsymbol{X}}{s_{F}}),s_{F}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{X}|)}{Z_{\max}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>q</mi><mtext>FP</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>nearest</mtext><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mi>𝑿</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝑿</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{FP}}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{\boldsymbol{X}}{s_{F}}),s_{F}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{X}|)}{Z_{\max}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the E4M3 grid, and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> is its maximum value. The scaling factor <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> is used for FP quantization (with the subscript <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> indicating the float type). The tensor <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{FP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>q</mi><mtext>FP</mtext></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{q}^{\text{FP}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>-bit FP quantized representation (FP8 in this paper). The corresponding dequantized tensor is given by:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}=\boldsymbol{X}^{\text{FP}}_{q}\cdot s_{\text{F}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑿</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝑿</mi><mi>q</mi><mtext>FP</mtext></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mtext>F</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\boldsymbol{X}}=\boldsymbol{X}^{\text{FP}}_{q}\cdot s_{\text{F}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When implementing quantization algorithms, it is essential to consider the specific characteristics of the target hardware. For example, a key optimization in Intel Gaudi 2 and 3 accelerators is that when both input tensors (i.e., weights and activations) use scaling factors that are powers of two, scaling can be efficiently implemented by adjusting the exponent bias instead of multiplying individual elements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. This reduces computational overhead and improves FP8 throughput by several percentage points.
To take advantage of this optimization, we incorporate the power-of-two scaling factors into our quantization scheme. For an in-depth analysis of using a power-of-two scaling factor, please refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, integer quantization is applied only to weight tensors for storage, while FP quantization is used for both weight and activation tensors at computation time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>PTQ - Main Challenges</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The quantization process in DNNs poses several fundamental challenges that must be carefully addressed when implementing PTQ algorithms. Below, we outline two key challenges relevant to our framework.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A primary issue is the presence of outliers, which force the scaling factor to accommodate an extended dynamic range. This results in the compression of most tensor values into a narrower range, increasing quantization step size and leading to higher reconstruction errors, which can significantly degrade model accuracy. To mitigate this, various techniques have been proposed, including clipping extreme values, per-channel or per-group quantization, and rotation methods that better capture the true distribution of values <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another key challenge in PTQ is that not all weights and activations contribute equally to the network’s final output. As a result, quantization errors in highly influential components can have a disproportionate impact on overall model accuracy. To address this, several strategies have been explored, including reordering the weight matrix based on activation magnitudes to prioritize more critical elements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, scaling weights and activations in a way that preserves the most important values while reducing errors in less significant ones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, and restoring key scalar values that have an outsized influence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.
These algorithms help maintain accuracy in quantized models by focusing on the most significant elements, ensuring a more robust and efficient quantization process.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now introduce our Dual Precision Quantization (DPQ) algorithm. DPQ follows a structured flow: first, high-precision weights are quantized to INT4 offline. During inference, the 4-bit weights are loaded and dequantized to FP8. Simultaneously, activations are quantized from brain float (BF) 16 to FP8 to leverage efficient FP8 matrix multiplication, with the output in high-precision (BF16).
To ensure clarity in the following formulation, we explicitly denote bit precision using subscripts to eliminate any ambiguity.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Note that our proposed target inference scheme involves two levels of weight quantization: 8-bit FP precision and 4-bit integer precision.
Each quantization step introduces an error due to the rounding operator, which can degrade the accuracy of the model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate this error, we take inspiration from the GPTQ algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and build upon the Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ) method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> for layer-wise quantization. Specifically, our objective is to find a 4-bit weight matrix, such that its dequantized 16-bit matrix, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑾</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}</annotation></semantics></math>, minimizes the squared error with respect to the full-precision BF16 layer output:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{argmin}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}}||\boldsymbol{W}_{16}\boldsymbol{X}_{16}-\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}\boldsymbol{X}_{16}||^{2}_{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>argmin</mtext><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑾</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>16</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑾</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>16</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{argmin}_{\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}}||\boldsymbol{W}_{16}\boldsymbol{X}_{16}-\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}\boldsymbol{X}_{16}||^{2}_{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝑾</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\boldsymbol{W}}_{16}</annotation></semantics></math> incorporates the two-step dequantization process: from INT4 to FP8, and then from FP8 to BF16, and will be formally defined later in this section. This ensures that the error in <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> accounts for the cumulative error introduced by both quantization levels, as this is the error that will be encountered during inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As in GPTQ, we quantize one weight at a time for each row in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{W}_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{W}_{16}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To mitigate the quantization error, we distribute the resulting error among subsequent weights in the row (i.e., from left to right). Each weight update is scaled by a factor determined by the Hessian matrix <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, which accounts for the importance of each weight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">We now provide a detailed description of the DPQ algorithm. First, we compute a scaling factor to convert the weights from BF16 to FP8, either per tensor or per channel. For clarity, we assume the scale is computed per tensor, denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{W}_{16}|)}{Z_{\max}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{W}_{16}|)}{Z_{\max}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.3" class="ltx_p">Next, consider the first weight in a given row of the weight matrix, denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{16}</annotation></semantics></math>. The procedure is applied independently to all weights in the first column, but we describe it for a single row for clarity. We quantize <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{16}</annotation></semantics></math> to FP8 using symmetric quantization:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{8}^{\text{FP}}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{w_{16}}{s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>8</mn><mtext>FP</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>nearest</mtext><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{8}^{\text{FP}}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{w_{16}}{s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.4" class="ltx_p">We then compute the per-group scale and zero-point for converting FP8 to INT4. These values are determined, for a given group <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> (which is represented in FP8 precision), once at the beginning of the group quantization process:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E8X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{\max(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})-\min(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})}{q_{\max}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>8</mn><mi>g</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>8</mn><mi>g</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{\max(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})-\min(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})}{q_{\max}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E8Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lceil{-\frac{\min(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})}{s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}}\rfloor}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>8</mn><mi>g</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lceil{-\frac{\min(\boldsymbol{W}_{8}^{g})}{s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}}\rfloor},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\max}=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\max}=15</annotation></semantics></math> for INT4 unsigned quantization as done in this paper.
Using the computed scale and zero-point, we quantize the weight to INT4 using asymmetric integer quantization:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{4}^{INT}=\lceil{\frac{w_{8}^{FP}}{s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}}+z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}\rfloor}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><mfrac><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{4}^{INT}=\lceil{\frac{w_{8}^{FP}}{s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}}+z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}\rfloor}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.6" class="ltx_p">The weight <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{4}^{INT}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{4}^{INT}</annotation></semantics></math> is the weight which will be stored and used in inference. Following OBQ, we now update the remaining weights in the row (which were not quantized yet), to compensate for the quantization error. This process includes few steps.
First, we dequantize the 4-bit weight back to FP8:</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}=(w_{4}^{INT}-z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g})\cdot s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}=(w_{4}^{INT}-z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g})\cdot s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.7" class="ltx_p">Then, we dequantize <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}</annotation></semantics></math> to BF16:</p>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{w}_{16}=\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}\cdot s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>8</mn><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{w}_{16}=\hat{w}_{8}^{FP}\cdot s_{w,16\rightarrow 8}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.8" class="ltx_p">We then compute the quantization error and scale it by the inverse of the corresponding diagonal element of the Hessian, denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}]_{qq}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>𝑯</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}]_{qq}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is the index of the currently quantized weight.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Next, let <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> denote the set of remaining full-precision weights, i.e., the weights positioned to the right of the currently quantized weight.
The optimal update for a weight <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{v}\in F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{v}\in F</annotation></semantics></math>, denoted by <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, is obtained by multiplying the scaled quantization error with the corresponding off-diagonal Hessian element <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1})_{q,v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑯</mi><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1})_{q,v}</annotation></semantics></math>, which captures the interaction between the quantized weight and the weight being updated: :</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="w_{v}\leftarrow w_{v}+\delta_{F},\quad\delta_{F}=-\frac{w_{16}-\hat{w}_{16}}{[\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1}]_{qq}}\cdot(\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1})_{qv}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn></msub></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑯</mi><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝑯</mi><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{v}\leftarrow w_{v}+\delta_{F},\quad\delta_{F}=-\frac{w_{16}-\hat{w}_{16}}{[\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1}]_{qq}}\cdot(\boldsymbol{H}_{F}^{-1})_{qv}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.2" class="ltx_p">The Hessian matrix characterizes the sensitivity of the weight to small perturbations, capturing how changes in the weight affect the loss function. The derivation of the optimal update in <a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> can be found in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This procedure is repeated iteratively for all remaining weights in the row.
A pseudocode for the proposed DPQ algorithm is provided in <a href="#algorithm1" title="In 3.3 Further Optimizations and Considerations ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Recall that our scheme also includes activation quantization. Specifically, the activation input <math id="S3.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{16}</annotation></semantics></math>, which serves as the input to the linear layer, is quantized to FP8 using symmetric quantization:</p>
<table id="S3.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{X}_{8}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{\boldsymbol{X}_{16}}{s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}}),s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{X}_{16}|)}{Z_{\max}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>nearest</mtext><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝑿</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{X}_{8}=\text{nearest}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\frac{\boldsymbol{X}_{16}}{s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}}),s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}=\frac{\max(|\boldsymbol{X}_{16}|)}{Z_{\max}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The scales <math id="S3.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{x,16\rightarrow 8}</annotation></semantics></math> are computed offline using a calibration dataset.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/GAR.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/126;" width="685" height="126" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of the GAR method. In this example, the weight tensor is divided into three groups, indicated by the red superscript. The black arrows represent the local ordering within each group, based on the diagonal elements of the Hessian for that group, while the red arrows denote the global ordering between groups, determined by the maximum diagonal Hessian element of each group. At the end of the quantization process, the tensor is re-permuted to its original order. Notably, scales operate on consecutive weights after the ordering process (as opposed to activation reordering done in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.)</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Inference-Aware Weight Reordering</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key challenge in the weight compensation approach is determining the optimal order for quantizing weights. The OBQ algorithm follows a greedy strategy, selecting the weight that introduces the least additional quantization error at each step. In contrast, GPTQ quantizes all rows in a predefined order. The original GPTQ paper proposes two schemes in the quantization process.
The first preserves the original order of weights within the tensor, and the second reorders weights based on the Hessian diagonal, prioritizing the quantization of ”more important” weights.
While the second approach improves accuracy, it introduces inference overhead due to the need of memory indexing in weight grouping. Specifically, the weights <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{W}_{8}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">W</mtext><mn>8</mn><mi>g</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{W}_{8}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> are consecutive in the permuted tensor, and thus the scales <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> and zero-points <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> operate on consecutive elements in the permuted tensor. However, the tensor saved and used in inference is the tensor in the original order, not the permuted tensor, and dequantizing online the weights using their pre-computed scales and zero-points can not be done in one multiplication as in the original case, thus increasing the inference latency (more details are given in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we propose Group-Aware Reordering (GAR), a reordering scheme that leverages Hessian information to prioritize important weights during quantization while avoiding inference overhead. GAR reorders weights under the constraint that weights can be permuted in one of two ways - within a group, and/or by moving whole groups. With GAR, scales operate on consecutive weights in the original order. This ensures that group-wise scales and weight groups remain consistent throughout inference.
Although GAR can also be beneficial for other methods, such as W4A16 GPTQ, it is especially helpful for DPQ. Without GAR, due to the nature of the predefined quantization order, alongside double quantization, large errors may accumulate in the weights which are quantized last. GAR reduces this error by quantizing the hard-to-quantize weights first, which then causes a reduced accumulated error to the latter weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> we demonstrate that our approach achieves higher accuracy compared to quantization without reordering and performs only slightly worse than unrestricted reordering while maintaining efficient inference execution.
An illustration of the GAR method is shown in <a href="#S3.F1" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and a detailed explanation of the scheme is provided in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.
<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3.2 Inference-Aware Weight Reordering ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides a high-level illustration of the proposed DPQ algorithm and <a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3.2 Inference-Aware Weight Reordering ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> provides an illustration of the inference flow under our W4A8 scheme.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/gar2.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:754/177;" width="754" height="177" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">High-level illustration of the proposed DPQ algorithm. We begin by hybrid reordering (GAR) of the weights based on their importance. Next, we apply two quantization levels: FP8 and INT4. The quantization errors from both processes are computed and distributed to the next, less ’important’ weights. Finally, we re-permute the tensor and the scales back to their original order.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/flow.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:617/178;" width="617" height="178" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of the inference flow of our proposed W4A8 scheme.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Further Optimizations and Considerations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further improve our quantization algorithm, we integrate additional techniques to enhance accuracy and efficiency.
First, the per-group scaling factor <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is determined by searching for the scale that minimizes the mean squared error (MSE). Additionally, we apply clipping to constrain values within the dynamic range of the low-precision tensor.
As done in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, we apply dampening to the Hessian matrix and employ the Cholesky decomposition for more efficient computation of the Hessian matrix in <a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="algorithm1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="algorithm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span>Dual Precision Quantization (DPQ)</figcaption>
<div id="algorithm1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_numbers_left ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="algorithm1.4.1" class="ltx_listingline">
<span id="algorithm1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> </span>Weight matrix <math id="algorithm1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{W}_{16}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝑾</mi><mn>16</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{W}_{16}</annotation></semantics></math> in BF16, Hessian matrix <math id="algorithm1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{H}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.2" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="algorithm1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text"><span id="algorithm1.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> </span>Quantized weight matrix <math id="algorithm1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{W}_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">W</mtext><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{W}_{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, scaling factors <math id="algorithm1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{16\rightarrow 8},s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{16\rightarrow 8},s_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math>, zero-point <math id="algorithm1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mi>g</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{8\rightarrow 4}^{g}</annotation></semantics></math>
</div>
<div id="algorithm1.4.3" class="ltx_listingline">

            Compute scaling factor <math id="algorithm1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{w,16\to 8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{w,16\to 8}</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S3.E6" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) ;
