<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we evaluate our proposed quantization and inference scheme in terms of both task accuracy and model performance (i.e., throughput).
All experiments were conducted on Gaudi 2 and 3 devices, with BF16 precision used as the baseline for performance comparison. The quantization experiments were implemented using Intel’s Neural Compressor framework<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          https://github.com/intel/neural-compressor</span></span></span>, an open-source toolkit for neural network compression.
We begin by evaluating visual reasoning on the MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, MMBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, and Math Vista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> benchmarks using the Qwen2-VL model family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, testing the 2B, 7B, and 72B models.
The tasks were evaluated using VLMEvalkit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> on Intel Gaudi 2.
Next, since the language component is a crucial aspect of large vision-language models, and since previous W4A8 methods have focused on it, we also evaluate our method on the Llama-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> and Llama-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> model families.
We evaluate the accuracy of our language models across three distinct categories: WikiText-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> for the measurement of perplexity, a comprehensive common sense reasoning suite, and MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite> for the assessment of broad knowledge. The common sense reasoning evaluation is comprised of the following: HellaSwag (HS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, LAMBADA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>, BoolQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, ARC Easy (ARC-e) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, PIQA (PQ) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, Winogrande (WG) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, ARC Challenge (Arc-c) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, and OpenBookQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>. Results are reported as the average normalized accuracy for all tasks. The language tasks were evaluated using the LM-Evaluation-Harness framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite> in a zero-shot setting to ensure consistent comparison between different experiments. Our code is publicly available.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The implementation of E4M3 in Gaudi 2 follows the IEEE standard for floating points, which reserves the largest exponent for NaN (not-a-number) and infinite values, and has the range of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 240" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 240</annotation></semantics></math>.
In Gaudi 3 the maximal exponent can be used for normal numbers, increasing the numerical range of E4M3 to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 448" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>448</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 448</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We used static (off-line) activation quantization, where the scaling factors are determined through calibration on the WebQuestions (WebQS) dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>, while the calibration set for the error compensation procedure in the weight quantization is a subset of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>.
In all our experiments, we use a group size of 128 for the INT4 asymmetric quantization, and a maximum sequence length of 2048. The FP8 scales are computed per tensor with symmetric quantization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, we quantize all linear layers to INT4, except for the embedding layer and the lm-head, as is common in other works. In the Qwen-VL model, we quantize all linear layer weights of the language model. Quantization times are similar to the timings reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Accuracy Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the WxAy notation to denote a quantization scheme in which weights are stored with <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-bit precision and activations with <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-bit precision. <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the results for the multi-modal dataset evaluated on the Qwen2-VL model family. The proposed DPQ algorithm demonstrates consistent performance across different model sizes and tasks, with only a minor degradation compared to the full BF16 reference. Notably, for most tasks, it outperforms the W4A16 GPTQ algorithm despite operating at a lower precision. This improvement can be attributed to the GAR method, which enhances model accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We next present a comparison of the proposed DPQ algorithm with state-of-the-art methods, including QServe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, QQQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, GPTQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, and the vanilla round-to-nearest (RTN) method on language tasks. The results for QServe and QQQ are taken directly from their papers, where we used the 128-group size configuration as in DPQ for a fair comparison. The GPTQ method is implemented without the FP8 error compensation used in DPQ (i.e., only the INT4 error is compensated).
<a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> demonstrates that DPQ outperforms both RTN and the naive implementation of GPTQ, as expected. Additionally, DPQ achieves better results than QServe and QQQ, which follow a different approach (both perform quantization to INT8 rather than FP8).
We also note that many optimizations in the QServe algorithm, such as block input/output module rotation and smoothing, are orthogonal to our method and could be integrated into DPQ to further increase its accuracy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the results for the WikiText-2, reasoning, and common sense tasks under various precisions.
As expected, schemes that quantize weights to 4 bits exhibit greater accuracy degradation compared to the W8A8 algorithm, due to the significantly lower bit representation. However, our proposed W4A8 DPQ algorithm achieves a reasonable accuracy degradation compared to the full precision model, and only a small accuracy degradation compared to the W4A16 scheme (in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> we implemented GPTQ with GAR, thus it serves as a natural upper bound for DPQ) while maintaining a more efficient trade-off between accuracy and latency (detailed in <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Performance Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>

The results for QServe and QQQ were taken from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, respectively.</span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy of language tasks under various precisions. The notations <math id="S4.T3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W4A16^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mn>16</mn><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W4A16^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W4A8^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W4A8^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> refer to schemes that use full activation reordering, which reduces accuracy degradation at the cost of increased latency. GPTQ (W4A16) is included in the results, since it is a common quantization algorithm. Also, since DPQ adds an additional level of quantization over GPTQ, it serves as an upper-bound to DPQ.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Performance Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using W4A8 improves model performance in several ways.
With respect to full FP8 quantization (weights and activations - W8A8) - using 4 bit weights allows to further reduce the memory footprint, thus allowing for larger models to fit into smaller or less devices (when using model parallel), and improves the memory bandwidth.
For example, using 4-bit weights allows models such as Llama 3.2 90B Vision to fit into a device such as Intel Gaudi 2 (96 Gb HBM) or Nvidia H100 (80Gb HBM).
With respect to 4-bit weight-only quantization (W4A16), using FP8 precision for the activations enables larger batch sizes (which yields faster overall tokens per second), and for faster GeMM operations, if the hardware has support for it (Gaudi 2, Gaudi 3, Nvidia H100, H200 have support for such).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To showcase the potential gains for the W4A8 format, we provide LLM model projections in <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.3 Performance Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. We analyze performance for various input and output lengths. Since many recent VLMs use both a Vision Transformer and an LLM, we focus on LLM performance, since the majority of compute and runtime is due to the auto-regressive LLM, rather than the ViT which runs once and is a fraction of the model.
We compare both 4 bit weights (W4A16) and FP8 quantization (W8A8), since both are popular quantization choices. Note that for the chosen models, a W16A16 (native BF16) model does not fit on a single device, thus not shown.
The speed-up is achieved by larger batch sizes (which are enabled by smaller model weights), as well as more efficient compute, due to the FP8 GeMM engines being used.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2505.14638v1/speedup_plots.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:754/628;" width="754" height="628"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Speed-up comparison between 3 methods on Gaudi 2 and Gaudi 3 accelerators. Each subplot compares speed-up of W4A8 (red) and W8A8 (blue) compared to W4A16 (green). The two upper plots compare Llama 2 70B on Gaudi 2 (left) and Gaudi 3 (right). The bottom plots compare Qwen 2 72B on Gaudi 2 (left) and Gaudi 3 (right). As can be seen, W4A8 can reach up to 3x speed-up over W4A16, and up to 1.4x speed-up over W8A8. W4A8 uses GAR, thus weights are consecutive in memory during inference. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct an ablation study to evaluate the impact of our proposed activation hybrid reordering GAR method on model accuracy. As discussed earlier, we expect this hybrid scheme to outperform the scheme without reordering. Although our method imposes constraints on the activation order, we note that most layers are characterized by a small number of highly important output activations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>. Consequently, even though our scheme only partially orders activations, it effectively captures the most significant weights. Thus, we expect only a slight accuracy degradation compared to the full reordering scheme.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our results, presented in <a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, support this hypothesis. Under both W4A16 and W4A8 quantization schemes, GAR yields a notable improvement over the scheme without reordering, while exhibiting only a minor accuracy degradation compared to full reordering scheme.
Note that GAR requires a ranking criterion to determine which group should be quantized first. In our experiments, we ordered groups based on their maximum Hessian diagonal element. Alternative criteria are possible, for example, ranking groups by the average of the top 10% largest elements before sorting. We leave the exploration of other ranking strategies for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another key insight into our algorithm emerges from the improved accuracy of DPQ compared to the naive implementation of GPTQ, as shown in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. DPQ mitigates nearly <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the accuracy degradation relative to the full-precision reference. This is because our method compensates for the error using the dequantized weight from both quantization levels, allowing it to account for both sources of error and produce a more accurate layer output. In contrast, a naive implementation of GPTQ in the W4A8 scheme introduces the FP8 quantization error on top of the compensated INT4 quantization error, resulting in the degradation observed in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

The scales for all methods are selected to minimize the mean squared quantization error between the dequantized and original tensors.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Discussion</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next discuss some key points regarding our work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The W4A16 scheme (when implemented with GAR as in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Accuracy Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), which only quantizes weights and performs computation in BF16, serves as a natural upper bound for our W4A8 approach . That is, we primarily compare our accuracy degradation against W4A16.
Optimizing W4A16 (weight-only) is beyond the scope of this paper.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our quantization method is orthogonal to many existing quantization strategies, such as AWQ, QuaRot, and others. Incorporating these techniques may further enhance our results. We leave this for future work.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce DPQ, a dual precision aware W4A8 quantization algorithm designed for efficient inference on modern accelerators. Our method leverages a two-step quantization process, mapping high-precision weights to INT4 and activations to FP8, enabling efficient FP8 matrix multiplication while minimizing accuracy degradation. We further enhance our approach with error compensation technique and Hessian-guided weight reordering, ensuring a good balance between performance and accuracy.
Experimental analysis on Qwen2-VL, Llama-2, and Llama-3 demonstrate that our W4A8 quantization method achieves significant throughput improvements while maintaining competitive accuracy relative to reference schemes.


<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we extend the description of the GAR method.
We consider the W4A16 scheme, i.e., when weights are quantized and stored in 4 bits, and computation is performed in BF16. The same rationale also applies to the W4A8 scheme discussed in this paper.
We begin by revisiting the quantization and dequantization process under the GPTQ algorithm when using per-group scaling and zero-point.
We then explain the rationale behind activation reordering, followed by a discussion on why unconstrained reordering introduces inference-time overhead. Finally, we present the proposed GAR method and explain how it improves accuracy without incurring any inference overhead.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Scales and Zero-Points Computation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We start by describing the computation of per-group scales and zero-points in the GPTQ quantization algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.
GPTQ operates iteratively, as described in <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.
While GPTQ is applied independently to all weights in the column, we describe it for some row <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> for clarity. The algorithm begins by computing the per-group scale and zero-point, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{i,1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{i,1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{i,1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{i,1}</annotation></semantics></math>, for converting weights of the first group from BF16 to INT4. These values are computed once at the beginning of the group quantization phase, using <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.1 Integer Quantization ‣ 2 Background ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Once <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{i,1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{i,1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{i,1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{i,1}</annotation></semantics></math> are computed, the first weight in the group, <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{i,1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{i,1}</annotation></semantics></math> is quantized to INT4 and then dequantized to BF16 using <a href="#A1.E14" title="In A.1 Scales and Zero-Points Computation ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>. The quantization error with respect to the original BF16 weight is then calculated and distributed to the remaining unprocessed weights in the same row (i.e., from left to right), following <a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>.
This process is then repeated for the second group, with a new set of parameters <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{i,2},z^{i,2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{i,2},z^{i,2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so on for each subsequent group. At the end of the quantization process, each group of weights has its own scale and zero-point, as shown in <a href="#A1.F5" title="In A.1 Scales and Zero-Points Computation ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, and the tensor is stored in its 4-bit representation, denoted by <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">At inference time, the stored 4-bit integer weights are loaded, and each group is dequantized to its 16-bit representation using the formula:</p>
<table id="A1.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{W}^{i,g}_{16}=(W_{4}^{i,g}-z^{i,g})\cdot s^{i,g}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>16</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mn>4</mn><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{W}^{i,g}_{16}=(W_{4}^{i,g}-z^{i,g})\cdot s^{i,g}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Since each scale and zero-point corresponds to a group of <span id="A1.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">consecutive</span> weights in the weight tensor, the dequantization for an entire group can be efficiently performed using a single multiplication and subtraction operation, leveraging vectorized computation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/group.png" id="A1.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/264;" width="685" height="264" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A1.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of per-group scale and zero-point. In this example, the weight tensor is divided into three groups, each containing two weights (i.e., a group size of 2).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Activation Reordering</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next describe the rationale behind activation reordering, its effect on the scaling factors and zero-points, and why this scheme results in inference-time overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The rationale for activation reordering can be explained as follows.
When using an iterative error compensation method, as described above and implemented in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and in this paper, it is beneficial to begin by quantizing the most ”important” weights. This is because the quantization error from the weights at the beginning of the row is propagated to later weights, which reduces the error for the earlier-positioned weights. Furthermore, the weights that appear at the end of the row accumulate more error due to previous updates, resulting in higher quantization error. Thus, weights that are quantized earlier will typically incur less quantization error.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To determine which weights are the most ”important”, we consider the diagonal of the Hessian matrix. These diagonal elements reflect the relative significance of different input features, as they correspond to the second-order sensitivity of the loss with respect to each weight, as explained intuitively next. Recall that for a linear layer with input <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, the Hessian under our objective in <a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3.1 Compensating for Quantization Errors in W4A8 Flow ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> is given by <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X^{T}X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X^{T}X</annotation></semantics></math>. In this case, the diagonal elements of the Hessian reflect the squared magnitudes of the input features. Consequently, weights associated with larger diagonal values contribute more significantly to the output. Modifying such weights has a stronger effect on the model’s behavior, making them more critical to quantize accurately.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Combining the above observations that (1) earlier-quantized weights incur lower error and (2) the most important weights are those associated with the largest Hessian diagonal entries, it is advantageous to reorder the weights with respect to the Hessian diagonal before the iterative quantization process. Specifically, this is done by permuting the Hessian in descending order with respect to its diagonal elements, and then reordering the weight tensor accordingly. This is precisely the activation reordering technique proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.
Empirically, this technique has been shown to enhance the accuracy of quantized models and is widely adopted in practice.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">However, despite its accuracy benefits, the reordering technique introduces additional overhead during inference (i.e., increased latency) as discussed next.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">When applying the activation reordering technique, we first permute the weight tensor and then run the iterative algorithm as described at the beginning of this section. Specifically, the scale factors and zero-points are computed for groups of the <span id="A1.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">permuted</span> weight tensor. At the end of the process, the weight tensor is re-permuted to its original order to ensure correct multiplication during inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">However, after re-permutation, the scale factors and zero-points are no longer aligned with the weight groups. That is, each weight in the tensor may now have a different scale and zero-point, as illustrated in <a href="#A1.F6" title="In A.2 Activation Reordering ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. As a result, the dequantization in <a href="#A1.E14" title="In A.1 Scales and Zero-Points Computation ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> can no longer be efficiently applied using a single scalar subtraction and multiplication per group. Instead, each weight must be individually processed with its corresponding zero-point and scale factor, increasing the number of operations required during inference and thereby increasing latency.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/act_order.png" id="A1.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/449;" width="685" height="449" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A1.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Computing scales and zero-points under full activation reordering scheme.
As can be seen in this example in the top matrix, the third and sixth columns have been reordered to the first and second columns. Thus during inference, their scale and zero point need to be fetched from these groups, which are not consecutive in memory, and require indexing.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Group Aware Reordering</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proposed GAR method addresses the issue of inference overhead while still allowing the weight tensor to be reordered based on weight importance, subject to certain constraints. Specifically, as described in <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Inference-Aware Weight Reordering ‣ 3 DPQ: Dual Precision Quantization for W4A8 ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, GAR allows permutations in two ways: (i) within a group, and/or (ii) by rearranging entire groups, as illustrated in the top panel of <a href="#A1.F7" title="In A.3 Group Aware Reordering ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This constrained permutation ensures that, after computing the scales and zero-points for the permuted tensor, each original group of weights shares the same scale and zero-point, as shown in the middle panel of <a href="#A1.F7" title="In A.3 Group Aware Reordering ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. As a result, when the weight tensor is re-permuted back to its original order, the associated scales and zero-points can be re-permuted accordingly (see the bottom panel of <a href="#A1.F7" title="In A.3 Group Aware Reordering ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). This guarantees that each group of weights retains its own scale and zero-point, allowing <a href="#A1.E14" title="In A.1 Scales and Zero-Points Computation ‣ Appendix A Group Aware Reordering (GAR) - Extended Description ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> to be efficiently implemented during inference, as in the original scheme without activation reordering.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.14638v1/figures/GAR_illustrated.png" id="A1.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:685/724;" width="685" height="724" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A1.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Computing scales and zero-points under GAR method.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although our method imposes constraints on the activation order, prior studies have shown that most layers are dominated by a small number of highly important output activations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>. Therefore, even though our scheme only allows a partial ordering of activations, it effectively preserves the most significant weights. As a result, we expect only a small accuracy gap compared to the full reordering scheme.
This hypothesis is supported by our results in <a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Dual Precision Quantization for Efficient and Accurate Deep Neural Networks Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Under both W4A16 and W4A8 quantization settings, the GAR method delivers a significant accuracy improvement over the baseline without reordering, while incurring only a minor accuracy drop relative to the full reordering approach.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we note that GAR requires a ranking criterion to determine which group should be quantized first. In our experiments, we ranked groups based on the maximum value of the Hessian diagonal within each group, that is, we compared the maximum diagonal entry of each group of weights. Alternative criteria are possible, for example, ranking groups by the average of the top 10% largest elements before sorting. We leave the exploration of other ranking strategies for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
